$comment: Gap fill, now a published pair. chem.glass-fiber and chem.silane were advertised by one fragment and named in another but never actually written by anyone; they are the canonical, reusable versions of two chains that several other fragments also carry short local copies of. Both are published via `shared`, so they are adopted into the tree even where nothing links them yet. chem.silane IS linked - many nodes in the silicon, logic and board fragments cite it, mostly as a `from` edge and once as a child - while chem.glass-fiber is currently reachable only through the generated unlinked.catalogue under c64.bottoms-out, because 20-board's laminate chain runs on its own local copy at mb.pcb.laminate.cloth.fibre.*.

chem.glass-fiber.name: E-glass fibre
chem.glass-fiber.description: Continuous glass filaments about 5 microns across, drawn in thousands from a tank furnace and woven into cloth. The C64 needs it twice on the board side of the machine: as the reinforcing cloth in the FR-4 mainboard laminate, and as the laminate core of the keyboard matrix board. E-glass is a lime-alumino-borosilicate, and the 15-19% of its weight that is not silica exists for one reason - it brings the working temperature down far enough that a 5 micron filament can be drawn from an affordable non-lead melt. That is why it is made in millions of tonnes a year and why it is the cheapest structural reinforcement known. Everything it is made of is weighed once, in a batch: silica sand, limestone, soda ash, a borate and a clay.

facts.label: E-glass composition
facts.value: typical analysis ~54 wt% SiO2, ~15% Al2O3, ~16% CaO, 0-10 wt% B2O3, 1-2 wt% Na2O+K2O, Fe2O3 under 0.5%

facts.label: Filament diameter
facts.value: about 5 um continuous roving; 9-24 um for chopped and mat grades

facts.label: Tensile strength / modulus
facts.value: 2-3.5 GPa / 70-76 GPa on the sized filament

facts.label: Softening point
facts.value: about 820 C, against a 1400-1500 C melt

chem.glass-fiber.note: Chopped strand for glass-filled phenolic connector bodies and glass-filled nylon is the same melt run through a hammer mill instead of a winder, so it shares this batch but not this filament.

chem.silane.name: Silane and organosilane chemistry
chem.silane.description: Monosilane, SiH4, is a gas made by redistributing trichlorosilane, and it is the precursor for the polysilicon films deposited inside the fab that made the 6510 and the 4164s. Organosilanes are the opposite: a methyl- or ethylchlorosilane that has been reacted with methanol or ethanol instead, so the molecule ends up carrying an alkoxy group and an organic group and is a liquid rather than a gas. They are the surface chemistry that bonds glass fibre to epoxy resin, and every FR-4 board in the world contains them. Both families come out of the same silicon-chlorine-hydrogen chemistry; that shared feedstock is the only relationship between them, and conflating the two is the usual first mistake.

facts.label: Shared feedstock
facts.value: trichlorosilane, from metallurgical silicon and HCl

facts.label: The split
facts.value: redistributing HSiCl3 gives SiH4, a pyrophoric gas; alkylchlorosilane plus alcohol gives RSi(OR')3, a liquid coupling agent

chem.silane.note: A statement about the supply chain rather than a substance: it covers monosilane gas and organosilane liquid chemistry together, and the two real materials hang beneath it.

chem.glass-fiber.borax.name: Borax (sodium borate)
chem.glass-fiber.borax.description: The boron source, and the reason E-glass is a borosilicate at all. Borax decahydrate, Na2B4O7.10H2O, goes into the batch either as the decahydrate or as boric acid made from it; either way the boron ends up in the glass network as B2O3. A few per cent of B2O3 lowers the liquidus and widens the working range enough to draw fine filament at a temperature the bushing alloy can survive, and it improves chemical durability - which is what stops the finished fibre dissolving in the warm caustic etch bath the board house puts it through.

facts.label: B2O3 in E-glass
facts.value: 0-10 wt% depending on the melt; the boron is what makes this a borosilicate

facts.label: Borax as batched
facts.value: Na2B4O7.10H2O (decahydrate, 47 wt% water) or calcined anhydrous, or as H3BO3

facts.label: Where the boron came from
facts.value: colemanite and ulexite ore, Turkey and California dominant by the 1980s

chem.glass-fiber.borax.note: Borax appears under other names elsewhere in the supply chain: tincalconite or boric acid for the electrolytic capacitor electrolyte, and a separate borax for the television funnel glass.

chem.glass-fiber.borax.ore.name: Colemanite and borate ore
chem.glass-fiber.borax.ore.description: The borates are mined from evaporite deposits and altered limestone-tuff beds, in Turkey (Bigadic, Emet) and California's Boron and Kramer districts. Ore is 25-35% B2O3 and is shipped as run-of-mine lump, so this is as close as the boron in a C64 mainboard gets to the ground.

facts.label: Principal districts
facts.value: Bigadic and Emet (Turkey); Boron and Kramer (California)

chem.silane.monosilane.name: Monosilane (SiH4)
chem.silane.monosilane.description: The polysilicon precursor: a colourless, pyrophoric gas that decomposes on a hot surface to lay down a conformal silicon film. A fab in 1982-84 that used it ran a small silane plant, because the gas is both too dangerous and too cheap to ship far. It goes into the machine's own logic: the polysilicon gate of the 6510, and the second of the three polysilicon levels in each 4164 DRAM, were deposited from silane by low-pressure CVD. It did not make the 9N polysilicon charge for the crystal pullers - that was still the Siemens trichlorosilane process until the late 1980s.

facts.label: Purity
facts.value: 4N-5N (99.99-99.9999%) electronic grade

facts.label: Boiling point
facts.value: -111.8 C, so it is handled as a liquefied gas

facts.label: Storage
facts.value: refrigerated bulk liquid in stainless or carbon-steel tanks at -60 C or below; cylinder supply at low pressure

facts.label: Hazard
facts.value: pyrophoric in air, acutely toxic, flammable from about 1% in air

chem.silane.coupling-agent.name: Organosilane coupling agents
chem.silane.coupling-agent.description: Bifunctional organosilanes: a hydrolysable alkoxy or chloro group that bonds to the silanol groups on a glass surface, and an organic group - vinyl, amino, epoxy or methacrylate - that reacts with the resin. Aminopropyltriethoxysilane and vinyltrimethoxysilane are the workhorses; methacryloxypropyltrimethoxysilane and 3-glycidoxypropyltrimethoxysilane were the ones chosen where the resin was an epoxy. They are made from the same silicon-chlorine chemistry as monosilane by substituting an alcohol for the hydrogen: methyltrichlorosilane plus methanol gives the trimethoxysilane and releases HCl. Applied to woven glass cloth at a few tenths of a per cent by weight, they are the reason epoxy bonds to glass rather than merely wetting it - and therefore the reason a C64 mainboard does not delaminate in a solder pot.

facts.label: Typical loading
facts.value: 0.3-1.0 wt% of the glass

facts.label: Preparation
facts.value: alkylchlorosilane plus methanol or ethanol, releasing HCl; the alcohol replaces the chlorine, not the hydrogen

facts.label: Form
facts.value: colourless to pale liquid, hydrolysed and condensed to a siloxane oligomer in the applied solution

facts.label: Competing chemistry
facts.value: titanate and zirconate coupling agents do the same job for glass-filled thermoplastics, without the silicon

chem.silane.coupling-agent.note: A coupling agent is a substance with a composition, and the operation that applies it to cloth is a separate step in the glass-fibre branch (chem.glass-fiber.cloth-sizing). Methanol is the route to the methoxy silanes, and the silicon-chlorine front end is the same one that makes trichlorosilane.

chem.glass-fiber.batch.name: Mix the batch
chem.glass-fiber.batch.description: The raw materials are weighed and dry-blended to about +/-1% on each constituent before a single tonne is melted. The tolerance matters more than it looks: the melt fixes the viscosity curve, and the viscosity curve decides whether 5 micron filament can be drawn from the bushing at all. A modern batch is tens of tonnes, and it is the last point at which the composition can be corrected.

facts.label: Batch size
facts.value: 1-40 tonnes

facts.label: Mixing time
facts.value: 2-8 minutes in a ribbon blender

facts.label: Target tolerance
facts.value: +/-1 wt% on the major constituents

chem.glass-fiber.batch.note: The five raw materials are children here rather than made-of edges: a glass batch is a mixture, so its constituents are siblings that melt into each other, and a reader following the chain needs to land on the sand and the limestone, not on a link list.

chem.glass-fiber.melt.name: Melt, refine and condition the batch
chem.glass-fiber.melt.description: The batch is charged into a regenerative tank furnace held at 1400-1500 C - hot enough to keep the viscosity low enough to draw a filament through a 10 micron hole, and then held in that narrow window for tens of hours. What comes out is not merely molten: it is refined until every bubble larger than a few microns has risen out or been broken by a rotating stirrer, and then conditioned - held just above the liquidus so that beta-eucryptite crystallises out on the refractory. That conditioning is the slowest step in the plant and the one that makes continuous fibre possible: without it the drawn fibre devitrifies into a crystalline, brittle mass the moment it cools.

facts.label: Refining bubble target
facts.value: no bubble above 1-50 um, depending on the grade

chem.glass-fiber.melt.note: Fuel was natural gas or fuel oil, and the two regenerators either side of the tank put 40-60% of the heat back into the incoming air, which is why a glass furnace is a net consumer of a few GJ per tonne of glass rather than a large one.

chem.glass-fiber.bushing.name: Forehearth and bushing plate
chem.glass-fiber.bushing.description: The glass leaves the furnace through a refractory forehearth and arrives at a bushing plate: a small alloy block, a couple of hundred millimetres across, drilled with 200 to several thousand holes of 10-40 microns. Gold-platinum-rhodium is the usual alloy because nothing else survives 1400 C in contact with a boron-bearing melt; the cheapest bushings are rhodium-plated nickel. Pressure pushes the melt through each hole, surface tension rounds the emerging cone, and gravity and attenuation do the rest.

facts.label: Bushing material
facts.value: Au-Pt-Rh alloy, or rhodium-plated nickel in the cheaper grades

chem.glass-fiber.attenuation.name: Attenuate and size the strand
chem.glass-fiber.attenuation.description: A blast of air at constant pressure across the wicket pulls the emerging cone out to about 5 microns before it has travelled half a metre, and the filament is wound onto a rotating package at 10-25 m/s. As it passes the sizing apron it picks up a thin film - starch or oil for the textile trade, and a light dose of silane for laminate grade. Continuous filament is not chopped: chopped strand is a separate product made by running the same strand through a hammer mill, which is what the glass-filled phenolic and glass-filled nylon parts elsewhere in this tree are made from.

facts.label: Filament diameter after attenuation
facts.value: about 5 um

facts.label: Strand length per package
facts.value: tens of kilometres

facts.label: Sizing on the strand
facts.value: starch or oil; a light silane for laminate grade

chem.glass-fiber.packaging.name: Spin, rove and weave the cloth
chem.glass-fiber.packaging.simple_name: Spin, rove and weave the cloth
chem.glass-fiber.packaging.description: The attenuated strand is wound onto a rotating package at high traverse speed, then a few hundred filaments are gathered into a roving and woven on an air-jet loom into plain-weave cloth. The loom is the reason a laminate is isotropic: a plain weave with a square fill puts equal glass in both directions, so the board does not creep along one axis when it is heated. That is why PCB cloth is woven rather than chopped or randomly matted. The kraft liner in the finished laminate panel is paper, not glass - a softwood pulp sheet - and belongs to the resin and liner branch, not here.

facts.label: Cloth weight for FR-4
facts.value: about 100-300 g/m2; roughly 200 g/m2 (style 7628, 7.9 oz/yd2) was the common one for 1.6 mm two-layer board

facts.label: Weave
facts.value: plain, or crow/twill where higher stiffness was wanted

facts.label: Yarn
facts.value: about 9-22 tex per 100 filaments, 8-18 filaments per cm of cloth

chem.glass-fiber.packaging.note: The 100-300 g/m2 range and style 7628 are the better-supported figures; the yarn tex and ends-per-cm figures are not checked against a 1983 laminate datasheet.

chem.glass-fiber.cloth-sizing.name: Size the woven cloth with silane
chem.glass-fiber.cloth-sizing.description: For laminate grade the woven cloth is desized and then treated with an organosilane coupling agent - sprayed or dipped, dried and cured at 100-150 C - before it is impregnated with epoxy. The molecule has one end that hydrolyses and bonds to the silanol groups on the glass surface and an organic end that reacts with the resin, so the glass is covalently joined to the epoxy instead of merely being wetted by it. That chemical bond across the cloth is what keeps a mainboard from delaminating along its own reinforcement when the assembly goes through a solder pot, and the 0.3-1.0 wt% of silane that buys it is invisible in the finished part.

facts.label: Loading
facts.value: 0.3-1.0 wt% of the glass

facts.label: Application
facts.value: spray or dip, then dry and cure at 100-150 C

facts.label: Effect
facts.value: an aminosilane-sized epoxy laminate shows roughly 20-50% higher apparent interlaminar shear strength than the same laminate on unsized cloth

chem.glass-fiber.cloth-sizing.note: The 20-50% interlaminar shear figure is a commonly quoted range for aminosilane versus no treatment rather than a measurement of a C64 panel, and the coupling agent used for a brominated-epoxy FR-4 was typically a methacrylate or glycidoxy silane rather than an amino one. The chemistry is the same in all three cases.

chem.glass-fiber.borax.acid.name: Boric acid from colemanite
chem.glass-fiber.borax.acid.description: Colemanite ore is crushed and boiled with sulfuric acid, which drives the calcium out as gypsum and leaves boric acid in solution: Ca2B6O11.5H2O + 2 H2SO4 + 2 H2O -> 2 CaSO4 + 6 H3BO3. The liquor is filtered hot and crystallised by cooling, and the crystals are dried at low temperature because boric acid dehydrates to B2O3 above about 100 C. Glass makers bought either this acid or the crude ash from dry lakes such as the ones at Boron and Kramer in southern California and at Bigadi in Turkey; the same boric acid is what the television-tube funnel glass borated, so that chain joins here. Searles Lake; the acid was the easier way to get a clean batch.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: colemanite + H2SO4 -> boric acid + gypsum, by boiling aqueous digestion

facts.label: Drying limit
facts.value: below about 100 C, or the acid dehydrates to B2O3

facts.label: Yield
facts.value: roughly 0.7-0.9 t of boric acid per tonne of 30% B2O3 ore

chem.silane.monosilane.tcs-route.name: Disproportionate the trichlorosilane
chem.silane.monosilane.tcs-route.description: The industrial route to monosilane: trichlorosilane redistributes into silane and tetrachlorosilane, catalysed, with the whole reaction run in a hydrogen atmosphere: 4 HSiCl3 -> SiH4 + 3 SiCl4. It suits a fab because the trichlorosilane it consumes is the same material the polysilicon plant already makes by the ton, delivered in bulk ISO containers or road tankers, and the tetrachlorosilane that comes back out is reclaimed by hydrogenation at the same plant. The silane leaves the reactor diluted to roughly a tenth or a quarter in hydrogen, which is what the crackers and the adsorption columns downstream were designed for and is far easier to handle than neat silane.

facts.label: Reaction
facts.value: 4 HSiCl3 -> SiH4 + 3 SiCl4 (disproportionation, run in H2)

facts.label: Crude output
facts.value: 10-25% SiH4 in H2, purified before use

facts.label: By-product
facts.value: SiCl4, hydrogenated back to trichlorosilane at the polysilicon plant

chem.silane.monosilane.tcs-route.note: This is a disproportionation of trichlorosilane, not a reduction by hydrogen - the hydrogen is the carrier and diluent gas, and the equation balances without it. Direct synthesis from metallurgical silicon and hydrogen also exists but was not the commercial route in this period.

chem.silane.monosilane.lpcvd.name: Deposit polysilicon by low-pressure CVD
chem.silane.monosilane.lpcvd.description: Silane decomposes on hot silicon in a diffusion tube at 600-850 C, laying down a conformal film of polycrystalline silicon. This is the step that changed how the C64's own chips were made. A self-aligned gate needs a gate material that survives ion implantation into the source and drain on either side of it, and that can be laid down and then oxidised around; aluminium can do neither, because it is destroyed by the implant and it diffuses into the oxide at the temperatures every later step needs. So once implantation replaced diffusion for source and drain doping, polysilicon won, and with it a gate that is chemically bonded to its own dielectric rather than merely resting on it.

facts.label: Film
facts.value: 100-500 nm of poly-Si, doped n+ or p+ from a gas in the same tube

facts.label: Reactor wall
facts.value: cold-wall quartz or silicon carbide tube; SiH4 decomposes appreciably above about 400 C, so a hot-wall tube would coat itself

facts.label: On the C64's own parts
facts.value: the 6510's gate, and the second of the three polysilicon levels in each 4164

chem.silane.monosilane.lpcvd.note: Dichlorosilane was the cheaper alternative and was used for the same films; silane won where the film had to be phosphorus- or boron-doped in the same step.
